To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the contribution of wood combustion to total BC is high in Switzerland (up to 33 % in winter) and that this fraction is well correlated with levoglucoson and potassium concentrations and with NOx.
wood burning contributes significantly to the total BC at the investigated sites and that the contribution of wood combustion to BC is well correlated to levoglucoson.

the contributions of wood burning and fossil-fuel to black carbon are well separable by multi-wavelength aetheralometer data, and that wood burning is an important source for black carbon in Switzerland.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantification of BC from WB emissions in Switzerland and its impact on the total BC load.
the quantification of BC from wood burning and FF combustion.
the quantification of BC from WB in urban and rural background sites in a highly industrialized country with a low share of WB in the energy supply.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
WB contributes to BC in Switzerland more than the contribution of wood combustion to the total final heat and energy production.
the contribution of WB to BC is overestimated when only the Angstrom exponent is used.
wood combustion is an important source of BC in Switzerland.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the contribution of WB to BC is higher in winter than during the summer and that the fraction of WB to total BC is highest in the rural area.
WB contributes on average about 25 % to BC at the considered Swiss sites, but this contribution is much larger during winter.
wood burning in Switzerland contributes to a significant extent to BC and that this is especially the case during winter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the contribution of WB to the total BC in the atmosphere is much higher than the share of wood burning to total energy consumption.
the source apportionment approach is a useful method to separate the contribution of WB and fossil fuel combustion to BC and to estimate the contribution of WB to total BC.
the contribution of wood smoke to BC in the atmosphere is higher than previously thought.
